beats.narration_text: Namasté. This is Liam, in for Bear. This film is about what Musinique is. It's an independent label, and now a free toolkit being built for indie musicians. The machine offers drafts and does the busywork. You listen, refine, and make the calls, on your own data. And the trap: thinking it's one more AI that writes your songs for you.

beats.motion_claim: TL;DR card one, WHAT: the question writes on and the three lines land on their spoken clauses.

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? For an indie artist, the scarce thing isn't songs. It's money and attention. Pay for the wrong playlist, and the streams can be fake and the money gone. Skip the release chores, and the song stays invisible. Get the decisions right, and a small budget goes where a record, not a feeling, says it can matter.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. A distributor is a service, like DistroKid, that delivers your song to the streaming platforms. Spotify for Artists is Spotify's dashboard of your own streams, listeners, and their cities. And playlist placement is a fee paid to get a song added to someone's playlist.

learn.question: Which of this week's jobs deserves the one small budget?
learn.action: Lay out the jobs, the offer and the budget.
learn.observation: Five jobs, one offer vouched for by a scanner, one bar of money.
learn.inference: Something has to decide, and it isn't obvious what.

beats.narration_text: Here's an artist with a finished song. Now the week begins. Lyrics to finish, a title to clean, release files for the distributor, a description and a bio. And an offer: pay for a playlist placement, and a scanner says the playlist is clean. There's one small budget. So which of these jobs deserves it, and on what evidence?

shot.visual_intent: The stage: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers). A waveform grows in the right panel under 'a finished song'; the five jobs land on their spoken clauses with a dim '?' in the who column; the budget bar grows full; a terracotta dot beside the playlist row; caption 'which job gets the money?'.
shot.motion_claim: The five jobs, the who column and the budget bar are the film's persistent objects; the unsolved case is who gets the money.

learn.question: Who finishes the lyrics?
learn.action: Run the same request through two artist profiles, then name what a draft still needs.
learn.observation: The drafts follow the profile; none of them is a finished song.
learn.inference: The machine can suggest from data; singing, hearing and rewriting are yours.

beats.narration_text: Start with the lyrics. Musinique keeps each artist as data: a profile with the voice, the languages, the genres. Ask for ideas as Aditi Banksy, and you get post-punk spoken word drafts in five languages. Swap in Mama Sparrow, same request, and you get lullaby sketches. But a draft isn't a song. You sing it, hear it, cut it, and rewrite it. The machine suggests. You finish.

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers). The lyrics row is spotlit; a profile card grows in the right panel (Aditi Banksy · post-punk · spoken word · five languages); it morphs into Mama Sparrow's (lullabies · close-miked soprano); a loop 'draft → hear → refine' draws under it with a return arrow; the lyrics row's tag becomes 'you finish'.
shot.motion_claim: Change one profile, watch the drafts follow; then the loop shows the finishing is human work.

learn.question: Who cleans the release?
learn.action: Apply the fixed title and lyric rules to a messy example.
learn.observation: The output is the same every time.
learn.inference: Rule-bound chores are execution; a test can prove them.
learn.next_question: So should the machine just do everything?

beats.narration_text: Now the release. A working title like this one: a version tag, the word final, a year. The stores want a clean title, so the machine strips it to 'A Freedom Riders Prayer'. Same with the lyrics: 'chorus, two times' becomes the chorus, written out twice. These rules are fixed, so a test can prove them. Again, the machine does it.

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers). The title row is spotlit; in the right panel a messy working title (constructed) gets its version tag, 'FINAL' and year struck through and collapses to 'A Freedom Riders Prayer'; '[Chorus 2x]' expands into two chorus lines; the title and files rows' tags become 'the machine'.

learn.question: Is Musinique an AI that does every job faster?
learn.action: Hand the playlist decision to the machine too.
learn.observation: The budget drains on the scanner's word.
learn.inference: Speed doesn't answer where the money should go.
learn.next_question: Then what kind of job is the playlist?

beats.narration_text: So is that the whole idea? An AI that does everything, faster? Let's try it. Hand every job to the machine, even the lyrics, even the playlist. The scanner said clean, so it pays. Watch the budget. Everything got faster, and the money still went to the one job that speed can't answer.

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers). The lyrics row and the last two rows flip to 'machine' in quick succession; the playlist row reads 'paid'; the budget bar shrinks to a sliver; a terracotta X beside it; caption 'faster work, same bad bet'.
shot.motion_claim: The natural wrong turn, walked: every job speeds up and the budget still drains.

learn.question: What kind of job is the playlist?
learn.action: Sort every job into execution or decision.
learn.observation: Four jobs are execution; the playlist is a decision.
learn.inference: Execution goes to the machine; a decision needs evidence and a person.
learn.next_question: What evidence does the decision have?

beats.narration_text: Back up. Here's the reframe. Every job is one of two kinds. Execution: clean the title, fill in the forms, draft the description. That's cheap now, and the machine should do it. Or a decision: which lyric is true, release this, pay for that. A decision needs a person, and evidence: your ear, your data. The machine can offer drafts for it, but Musinique sorts every job into one of those two kinds.

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers). The budget refills (rewind); an execution bracket draws beside the three chore rows; decision marks draw beside the lyrics row ('your ear') and the playlist row ('your data'); the lyrics tag returns to 'you finish' and the playlist lands on 'you decide' with a terracotta dot.
shot.motion_claim: The representation: every job is execution or a decision, and only a decision can protect the budget.

learn.question: With your own data on screen, pay or skip?
learn.action: Put the scanner's verdict beside your Spotify for Artists numbers.
learn.observation: The viewer commits to an answer.
learn.inference: A prediction makes the next beat evidence.

beats.narration_text: So look at the playlist with your own data. The scanner says clean. Your Spotify for Artists page says the playlist has about a dozen followers, sends you hundreds of streams a day, and the top city is Ashburn, Virginia. Before it moves: pay, or skip?

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers), split. The right panel fills with evidence rows: 'the scanner: clean' (dim), then 'followers · about a dozen', 'streams · hundreds a day', 'top city · Ashburn, Virginia' (example numbers, captioned); a terracotta dot; caption 'commit: pay, or skip?'; hold.
shot.motion_claim: Predict before the reveal: the objects hold while the viewer commits.

learn.question: Pay or skip?
learn.action: Apply the data-center gate to the evidence.
learn.observation: The gate vetoes the payment; the budget stays full.
learn.inference: A gate on your own data outranks the scanner's verdict.
learn.next_question: So what is Musinique, in one line?

beats.narration_text: Skip. Ashburn is one of the world's biggest data-center hubs, and a dozen followers rarely explain hundreds of plays a day. In the plan, a data-center city is a gate, not a vote. It vetoes the payment, whatever the scanner said. And look at the budget. It never moved.

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers), split, evidence up. 'top city' morphs to 'a data-center hub'; a terracotta X lands by 'the scanner: clean'; an ink gate bar drops across the playlist row; the row rewrites to 'Skip this playlist'; the full budget bar is indicated.
shot.motion_claim: The collision: one fact from the artist's own data vetoes the spend, and the budget the naive run lost stays whole.

learn.question: What is Musinique, in one line?
learn.action: Name the rule behind every sort; route brand and video out.
learn.observation: Every job fell to the machine or to you; two kinds of work leave for the neighbors.
learn.inference: The machine executes, you decide on your own data; Madison and brutalist.art handle brand and video.

beats.narration_text: That's what Musinique is. The machine does the chores and suggests drafts. You listen, decide, and finish, on your own data. It doesn't try to do everything itself. Brand and copy go to Madison. Video goes to brutalist dot art. Musinique keeps the part in the middle: what to make, what to release, and where the money goes.

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers), split, gate down. Evidence clears; 'the machine suggests · you decide' lands bold under the columns; two ink arrows draw from the right panel to 'Madison · brand and copy' and 'brutalist.art · video'; the middle labelled 'Musinique: what to make, release, and fund'.
shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives as the name for every sort we just watched, and the two neighbors take what Musinique doesn't do.

learn.question: So which job deserved the budget?
learn.action: Return to the hook's week, resolved.
learn.observation: Every row is done and the budget is whole.
learn.inference: The machine took the chores; the decision kept the money.

beats.narration_text: Back to our artist. Same song, same week. The chores are done by the machine, the lyrics are yours, finished by ear, and the budget is still there for something the evidence supports. One honest note: Musinique is a plan today, and the build is just starting. Not taught here: how the audit weighs each piece of evidence. That's your turn.

shot.visual_intent: the week's jobs left (five rows), 'who does it' tags middle, a right panel for the case at hand, the budget bar bottom right (ink fill, no numbers). The hook view returns: the waveform, the five rows, each now ticked with an ink dot; the budget bar full; caption 'same week · money kept'; a dim boundary caption 'a plan today · not taught: how the audit weighs evidence'.
shot.motion_claim: The HOOK's objects resolve: same week, busywork done, the money kept for a decision the evidence supports.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Musinique is an independent label, and a free toolkit being built for indie musicians. The machine suggests lyric drafts and does the chores: clean titles, release files. You hear, refine, and decide, on your own data, and a gate vetoes a bad spend. Brand and copy go to Madison. Video goes to brutalist dot art.
